2348-the-disappearance-of-lady-frances-c:
Holmes is called to find Lady Frances Carfax, a lonely aristocrat who has vanished on the Continent, leaving only a trail of hotels and a coffin. Arthur Conan Doyle sends Watson ahead to investigate, then brings Holmes to rescue the lady from a villainous couple's murderous plot. The story's tension builds through Watson's reports from abroad.

The case turns on a false funeral and a race against burial alive. It is a late Holmes adventure with real suspense. Readers will enjoy Watson's unusually central role. Watson's solo work in this case shows how much he learned from Holmes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abrasax:
Abrasax is the true name, not Abraxas, of a class of small ancient stones carved with strange figures and formulas. Many of them still resist interpretation, and specimens sit in almost every museum and private collection. The spelling Abraxas arose from Latin confusion between Sigma and Xi. Among early Gnostics the word carried several meanings, and Basilides gave the title to Almighty God, claiming its letters add up to 365, the number of the solar cycle.

It is an error, the entry insists, to call every Gnostic stone an Abrasax, just as Jupiter and Venus do not name every ancient statue. Abrasax names the Supreme Deity in Gnostic thought, not talismans in general. Very many secrets of Gnosticism remain unexplained, the entry admits, but hopes they will not stay shrouded in mystery. It points readers to King, Bellermann, Dieterich, and Matter.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dax:
A diocesan entry describes Dax, an ancient French see suppressed under the Concordat of 1801, its territory now split between Aix and Bayonne. Its patron, the martyr Vincent, may not have been a bishop, though his cult existed in Charlemagne's time. The oldest martyrdom account comes from a thirteenth-century Dax breviary, and excavations found a Merovingian cemetery on a church site dedicated to Vincent by Bishop Gratianus.

Gratianus, present at Agde in 506, is the first historically known bishop. Later bishops included Revellatus, Macarius, and Cardinals Itier and Foix, founder of Avignon University and Toulouse's College de Foix. Dax's synodal constitutions, published by Abbe Degert, illuminate thirteenth- and fourteenth-century church customs, and Vincent de Paul first studied there with the Cordeliers about 1588.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-halifax:
Nova Scotia's Archdiocese of Halifax takes its name from the capital founded by Lord Cornwallis in 1749 and covers the province's middle and western counties with Bermuda, attached since 1851. Its story opens at Port Royal, founded by De Monts in 1604. Mass was first offered there on what is now Canadian soil.

French Jesuits, Recollects, and Capuchins worked among settlers and Micmacs until the Acadian expulsion of 1755, and penal laws kept Catholics down until Irish petitioners won repeal in 1783. A vicariate in 1817 became a diocese in 1842 and an archdiocese in 1852, under bishops Burke, Fraser, Walsh, and Connolly, the last a champion of confederation and foe of Fenianism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maximinus-thr:
Maximinus Thrax, Roman emperor from 235 to 238, was the son of a Goth and an Alanic mother. A shepherd of huge size and strength, he caught Septimius Severus's eye in a contest with soldiers during the emperor's passage through Thrace in 202 and joined the body-guard. He refused to serve under Macrinus and Heliogabalus, but Alexander Severus gave him command of new Pannonian troops.

Those troops, wanting a real warrior rather than the timid young Alexander, ruled by his mother Julia Mamaea, proclaimed Maximinus emperor at Mainz in March 235, with his son Maximus as co-regent. He campaigned with vigour across the Rhine, regained the Agri Decumates, and beat Sarmatians and Dacians on the Danube, taking the names Germanicus and Sarmaticus. He taxed and executed patricians freely, melted temple bronze for coin, and showered revenues on his devoted soldiers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pax:
Pax, also called osculatorium or tabula pacis, is a tablet for giving the peace. The Church's primitive usage was the holy kiss given freely. Later, under the Apostolic Constitutions, lay men kissed men and women kissed women. That lasted till the thirteenth century, when a substitute appeared: a tablet or plate bearing the Blessed Virgin, the church's titular, or most often the crucifixion.

The earliest notice of them lies in thirteenth-century English council records. Cardinal Bona credits the Franciscans with the departure. Kissed by the celebrant and wiped with linen, the tablet was carried to others to kiss. The rite holds in low Masses, giving peace to prelates and princes, rarely to others by custom. The acolyte at the celebrant's right presents the tablet. The celebrant kisses it saying Peace be with you. The server answers, And with your spirit.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pertinax:
Pertinax was a Roman emperor whose reign lasted barely three months in 193. A freedman's son born at Alba Pompeia in 126, he taught grammar at Rome before joining the army. Ability in war and civil office won him praetorship, consulship, and commands along the Danube under Marcus Aurelius, governorships of Moesia, Dacia, and Syria, and later the prefecture of Rome under Commodus.

After Commodus was strangled, soldiers proclaimed Pertinax emperor at the praetorian prefect's urging, and the Senate confirmed him. He revived the title Princeps Senatus and took the name Father of his Country. Selling Commodus's costly plate and furniture, he paid the guards, resumed public works, recalled the banished, and tried informers. He died at Rome on 28 March 193, after ruling from the last day of 192.

max: Katherine Cecil Thurston wrote Max, a novel printed by Harper in 1910. Frank Craig drew the pictures, and one shows a figure in a Petersburg court. The hosted sample preserves the front pages and the picture list only. No readable chapter text appears beyond the head of part one. This note stays with the title, the author, and the year for that reason. The plot cannot be described from the sample held here.
nasa-tm-19720024218-a-model-of-the-local: A model of the local region of the galaxy is a NASA technical memorandum on space near the Sun. The hosted sample is garbled optical character text, and it preserves no readable author name, center, or date. Its abstract, kept with the record, describes a two part model of matter between the stars. The model rests on low radio waves picked up by the Radio Astronomy Explorer satellite. It points to a thick spiral arm and a thick layer tied to electrons.
the-disappearance-of-lady-frances-carfax:
Sir Arthur Conan Doyle opens The Disappearance of Lady Frances Carfax on a small deduction. But why Turkish? asks Sherlock Holmes, gazing fixedly at Watson's boots, as Watson reclines in a cane-backed chair with his feet out. Watson answers that the boots are English, bought at Latimer's in Oxford Street.

Holmes corrects him: he meant the bath. Why the relaxing, costly Turkish bath rather than the brisk home-made kind? Watson pleads rheumatism and age; a Turkish bath is an alterative, a fresh starting-point, a cleanser of the system. He then asks Holmes to show the link between boots and bath. Holmes points to splashes on the left sleeve and shoulder of Watson's coat. Had he sat in the center of a hansom, the splashes would be few or balanced. So he sat at the side, and he had a companion in the cab that morning.
the-vicissitudes-of-bessie-fairfax: Holme Lee, the pen name of Harriet Parr, wrote The Vicissitudes of Bessie Fairfax, issued at Philadelphia by Porter and Coates. An epigraph warns that life gives not what we wish but what we must put up with. Only the title page and a partial contents list are present here, so the novel itself does not appear. Chapters trace Bessie's birth and parentage, a lawyer's letter, the community of Beechhurst, and a fate sealed against her inclination. Later headings promise school-days at Caen and a family secret.
uncle-max: Rosa Nouchette Carey's Uncle Max, dated 1894, survives here through its contents. The chapters open Out of the Mist, then move behind bars to a Cinderella, and Uncle Max breaks the ice in chapter four. Later titles promise a flag of truce, a difficult patient, one of God's heroines, and a missed vocation. Only the title page and contents are present here, so the novel itself does not appear.
